{"id": "17:70/q03", "question": "In what does God's honoring of humanity consist?", "turns_on": "Whether a single distinctive faculty or bodily feature defines honor, or the verse gathers multiple gifts.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q03/p1", "position": "It comprises many bodily, intellectual, spiritual, and practical gifts rather than one exclusive trait.", "reasons": "Zajjāj adds guidance and provision to bodily traits; Ṭabrisī prefers the whole range. Bayḍāwī and Nasafī list form, temperament, reason, speech, writing, guidance and crafts. Rāzī calls the human soul and body the noblest in the lower world, analyzes its vegetative, animal and rational powers and the upper origin of spirit, and cites 24:35, 96:1–4 and 82:6; Abū Ḥayyān objects that this philosophical idiom is foreign to Arabic expression. Biqāʿī says the omitted object of honoring generalizes it. Bursevī gives bodily and spiritual strata; Ibn ʿĀshūr adds cleanliness, dress, self-awareness, craft and civilization. Ālūsī rejects restricting honor to reason alone; Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes intellectual products from particular comparative advantages."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p2", "position": "The chief distinction is intellect, discernment and knowledge of God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports reason; Junayd, Jaʿfar and Abū ʿUthmān stress understanding or gnosis. Rāzī calls rational knowledge higher than animal powers and references twenty arguments at 24:35. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurṭubī prefer reason because it enables knowledge of God, revelation and bliss; Qurṭubī compares reason to the eye and law to the sun. Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes animals can exceed people in speed, strength, courage or senses. Biqāʿī analyzes the soul's faculties; Asad invokes conceptual thought and 2:31."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p3", "position": "Humans eat and drink with hands or fingers, unlike animals that use their mouths.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj adds work and manipulation; Jābir's report names fingers. Rāzī and Nasafī relate Abū Yūsuf's citation to al-Rashīd, who then put away his spoon. Ibn ʿĀshūr includes lifting water or utensils. Ibn al-Jawzī contrasts human clean food with jinn eating bones and dung. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says hand eating alone is inadequate because animals excel elsewhere."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p4", "position": "Humans have speech, expressive communication and discernment.", "reasons": "Rāzī says humans can define and convey inward experiences; a mute person can gesture or write, whereas a parrot only imitates. Biqāʿī notes the progression from life to speech. Ḍaḥḥāk's reports sometimes name speech alone and sometimes speech with discernment."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p5", "position": "Humans have upright, proportioned stature and bodily beauty.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites 40:64, 23:14 and 2:138, including the arrangement of the eye; he says height alone fails since trees are taller. Reports also single out men's beards and women's tresses or forelocks. Biqāʿī adds dexterous reach; 95:4 supports Ibn Kathīr's account; Jābir's report contrasts upright humanity with bent creatures."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p6", "position": "God gave people mastery over other creatures and subjected creation to their use.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and Ibn Jarīr relate mastery to transport and lawful food; Rāzī details earth, water, air, fire, minerals, plants, animals and sea with 20:55, 2:22 and 16:14, plus a winter poem. Ibn Kathīr and Study Quran cite Adam's creation by God's Hands, divine breath, and taught names (38:75; 15:29; 2:31)."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p7", "position": "God honored humanity by placing Muhammad among them or the best community within them.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb is repeatedly named for the Prophet; Māwardī and Baghawī mention the best community, whose collective description Ṭabrisī links to 3:110."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p8", "position": "Honor lies in writing and accumulated learning.", "reasons": "Rāzī says writing preserves earlier scholarship and expands science, virtue and religion, citing teaching by the pen at 96:3–5."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p9", "position": "Humanity is honored by divine address, moral commands and prohibitions, messengers and revelation.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr ibn Ṭāhir stresses direct divine commands; al-Ḥusayn adds being held in God's grasp and addressed; Sulamī also reports the gift of messengers. Bursevī distinguishes covenant, fitra and revelation shared by all from special faith or prophethood."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p10", "position": "Honor is divine kindness and provision preceding human request or obedience.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says God meets needs before prayer, giving and answering first. Māwardī speaks of God's beneficence; Zayd ibn Aslam singles out foods and pleasures."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p11", "position": "Honor is a beautiful human voice.", "reasons": "Dhu al-Nūn gives this specific answer."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p12", "position": "Honor consists in God creating Adam by His Hand.", "reasons": "Rāzī says this implies greater care than creation by 'Be'; Study Quran connects the Hands with the breathed Spirit and extraordinary knowledge, citing 38:75, 15:29 and 2:31."}, {"id": "17:70/q03/p13", "position": "Honor lies in Adam's inherited divine form.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports the proposal that Adam was created in the form of the Merciful and transmitted this inheritance."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q04", "question": "What does being carried on land and sea describe?", "turns_on": "Whether carriage names mounts and ships, protection from sinking, or an inward passage.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q04/p1", "position": "People ride animals on land and ships at sea.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās names camels, horses, mules and donkeys; Ibn al-Jawzī and Ālūsī call these soft backs and ships dry boards. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls ship carrying a metaphor from riding, cites 69:11, and adds God-taught sails and oars. Rāzī adds travel, defense, war and livelihood; Kuranyolu extends the benefit to trade and modern transport. Ālūsī prefers this because it uniquely distinguishes humans."}, {"id": "17:70/q04/p2", "position": "God keeps people settled upon land and water instead of allowing them to sink or drown.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī offers this alternative; Ālūsī reports and rejects its distinctiveness, since other creatures also avoid sinking."}, {"id": "17:70/q04/p3", "position": "Land and sea signify body or self and spirit or heart in an inward journey.", "reasons": "Sulamī says self and heart need the light of divine support, otherwise planning fails; Wasitī calls them manifest attributes and hidden realities, another saying separation and union. Qāshānī reads bodily and spiritual travel toward perfection. Bursevī's Najmī source makes the destination the shore of lordship and reports knowledge and unity."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q05", "question": "Why does the verse mention travel on land and sea?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrasing is explained by the historical reach of transport, its surrounding context, or its moral effect.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q05/p1", "position": "They are the forms of travel shared across humanity and fit the surrounding land and sea passage.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī says no air travel existed at revelation, the past verbs address historic gifts, saying only air would exclude many, and 17:66–68 concerns land and sea."}, {"id": "17:70/q05/p2", "position": "The familiar means of transport are recalled to invite gratitude and reflection on divine power.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu says everyday familiarity hides the significance of trade and travel; Study Quran connects mounts and ships with gratitude."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q06", "question": "What are the ṭayyibāt provided to humanity?", "turns_on": "Whether ṭayyib describes taste, lawfulness, useful benefit, or an inward gift.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q06/p1", "position": "Pleasant, choice foods and drinks, especially prepared human fare.", "reasons": "Examples vary: bread, meat, honey, clarified butter, butter, dates, sweets, fruit, grains, livestock, crops, milk and drinks. Damghānī cites 40:64 and 16:114; Ibn Kathīr adds fine sights and clothes, including goods brought from afar. Rāzī stresses purification and cooking; Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses knowledge of appealing varieties and human invention."}, {"id": "17:70/q06/p2", "position": "They are lawful or permitted provisions.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUthmān and Ibrāhīm al-Khawwāṣ say lawful; Māwardī, Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān transmit the same sense. Kuranyolu combines lawfulness with appeal and advises healthy, clean, aesthetically good lawful provision."}, {"id": "17:70/q06/p3", "position": "They encompass all useful resources, including earnings, clothes, furnishings and possessions.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says provision is anything beneficial and contrasts human earning and dress with animals. Sahl names beneficial worker's earnings; Nasafī offers what one's hands earned. Ālūsī includes desirable goods obtained by work or otherwise."}, {"id": "17:70/q06/p4", "position": "They are sincere deeds recorded for the worker.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Mubārak specifies written deeds done sincerely."}, {"id": "17:70/q06/p5", "position": "They are things arriving without request or expectation.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh gives this inward criterion."}, {"id": "17:70/q06/p6", "position": "For the elect they are witnessing, unveiling, knowledge and love.", "reasons": "Bursevī's Najmī source pictures food of witnessing and drink of unveiling in vessels of gnosis and cups of love, surpassing even near angels."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q07", "question": "Should one renounce pleasant food because of this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether deprivation follows a sound report and serves health and worship.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q07/p1", "position": "No; suitable pleasant food may be eaten and the body cared for.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī says the report attributed to ʿĀʾisha about Satan and tasty food has no basis and authentic Sunnah contradicts it. His scholars call severe deprivati

on contrary to wisdom, law and reason: wheat is given to people, husks to livestock; bran, barley and coarse salt may harm health. He cites 57:27 against invented monasticism, and examples of Ibn Adham and al-Thawrī eating fine food then worshipping."}, {"id": "17:70/q07/p2", "position": "Ascetic refusal of ordinary or refined food is practiced or commended.", "reasons": "Some Sufis invoke the ʿĀʾisha report; stories say Sahl lived on nabq and fig leaves, Dhu al-Nūn rejected finely ground salt and bread for barley, and Abū Yazīd avoided others' food for forty years. Qurṭubī disputes the practice."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q08", "question": "What kind of preference over creatures is asserted?", "turns_on": "Whether preference concerns worldly advantage, reward and virtue, or inward perfection.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q08/p1", "position": "It is observable human mastery, use, and advantage over earthly creatures.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī emphasizes dominance over subjected beasts; Ibn ʿĀshūr limits this to reason and ingenuity in the visible world. Qurṭubī adds reward, protection, discernment and insight; Māwardī and Bayḍāwī list dominance as one possible sense. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kuranyolu deny that the statement decides unseen ranks."}, {"id": "17:70/q08/p2", "position": "It is reward, spiritual rank, or virtue attained through faith and obedience.", "reasons": "Māwardī gives reward; Abū Ḥayyān reports afterlife reward. Ibn al-Jawzī's Ibn ʿAbbās report restricts the favored humans to believers. Nasafī says reason mastering desire elevates a human above angels, while surrender to desire lowers one below beasts. Biqāʿī names the pious elect."}, {"id": "17:70/q08/p3", "position": "It is preservation, discernment and penetrating insight.", "reasons": "Māwardī gives separate formulations: protection and discrimination, or acquired insight or physiognomic perception; Sulamī reports discernment, self-knowledge and accurate spiritual insight."}, {"id": "17:70/q08/p4", "position": "It is nobility or honor itself.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī offers nobility alongside dominance; Ālūsī reports an identification of preference with the already mentioned honor."}, {"id": "17:70/q08/p5", "position": "It is the human capacity to combine intellect and appetite and grow toward perfection.", "reasons": "Rāzī divides beings into intellect without appetite, appetite without intellect, neither, and both; humans surpass beasts. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says developing humans may reach beyond angels, citing Adam's knowledge at 2:30."}, {"id": "17:70/q08/p6", "position": "It is an inward perfection of unity and direct receptivity to divine light.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says prophets' superiority stems from entrusted divine knowledge rather than mere species membership, citing 2:30. Bursevī's Najmī commentary cites 33:72 and 24:35 for the perfect human as bearer of trust; Kashifī likens that human to a mirror collecting divine attributes."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q09", "question": "Who are the 'many' over whom humanity is preferred?", "turns_on": "Whether kathīr is literal or rhetorical, whether min is partitive or explanatory, and whether exclusion entails rank.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q09/p1", "position": "Many means animals and sometimes jinn within the created material order; angels are outside the comparison.", "reasons": "Suddi names beasts; Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes animals and jinn. Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites animal communities at 6:38 and calls angels noncosmic beings. Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī say exclusion alone leaves angelic rank undetermined. Ibn ʿĀshūr says revelation, not this observable comparison, establishes unseen ranks."}, {"id": "17:70/q09/p2", "position": "Many is literal and excludes all angels from human superiority.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Naḥḥās argue angels exceed people in obedience and freedom from sin, with 4:172 cited. Zamakhsharī attacks a universal reading; some infer even prophets fall below angels. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Rāzī, Ṭabrisī and Abū Ḥayyān reject the inference from mere exclusion."}, {"id": "17:70/q09/p3", "position": "Many is literal, but only selected leading angels are excepted.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī names Gabriel, Michael, Israfil, the Angel of Death/Azrail and peers; one Ibn ʿAbbās report also exempts some leading angels. Bayḍāwī leaves open whether all or only elect angels are outside the group."}, {"id": "17:70/q09/p4", "position": "Many functions rhetorically as all creation, including angels.", "reasons": "Ṭhaʿlabī and Ibn al-Jawzī cite 'most' for all devils at 26:223; Baghawī cites 26:221–222; Nasafī attributes the universal reading to al-Ḥasan. Ṭabrisī allows this in rebuttal; Study Quran invokes angels' prostration to Adam (2:34 and parallels). Zamakhsharī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bayḍāwī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī object that this is strained or inelegant."}, {"id": "17:70/q09/p5", "position": "Min is explanatory: humanity exceeds all intelligent creatures, including angels and jinn.", "reasons": "Ṭībī says a kind cannot exceed itself. Ālūsī objects that explanatory min is remote and abandons the usual partitive reading."}, {"id": "17:70/q09/p6", "position": "The many may itself be the numerous angels among rational creatures.", "reasons": "Al-Taqrīb proposes this; Ālūsī accepts the possibility that the preferred-over group is strong, not an automatic exception."}, {"id": "17:70/q09/p7", "position": "Min is partitive, but mentioning many does not determine the remainder's size or rank.", "reasons": "Ṭībī compares 2:253, where preferring over many honors the many. Ālūsī contrasts contextual 'some guided, many disobedient' at 57:26 with unopposed 'many' at 27:15, which need not mean a majority; he rejects arguments based solely on an alleged angelic exclusion."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q10", "question": "How do humans and angels rank in relation to one another?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse compares spiritual rank at all, and how nature, free choice, prophethood and angelic classes bear on rank.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q10/p1", "position": "The verse does not settle the human–angel ranking.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says angels can be superior or equal without being among the many, while 4:172 gives separate evidence. Rāzī calls proof from the verse's implication weak. Ṭabrisī says worldly blessings differ from reward and angelic classes may outrank humanity while individual prophets excel. Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān likewise leave the comparison open; Ālūsī disputes the probative force of implication. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kuranyolu limit the verse to observable dominion."}, {"id": "17:70/q10/p2", "position": "Angels generally outrank human beings.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Naḥḥās point to sinless obedience and 4:172. Zamakhsharī reads kathīr as excluding angels and calls contrary reports fabricated; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says angels' pure nature and sincere worship exceed mixed human nature and rejects reducing their obedience to mechanical behavior, citing 21:26–28, 66:6, 41:38 and 7:205. Rāzī recognizes the argument but finds this verse weak proof."}, {"id": "17:70/q10/p3", "position": "Believers or righteous humans surpass angels.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra's report says a believer is dearer than near angels; Baghawī chooses ordinary believers over ordinary angels and elite believers over elite angels, citing 98:7. Nasafī reasons that reason mastering desire raises humans, while vice lowers them below beasts. Ashʿarī and Shiʿi advocates cite choice against temptation; Ṭabāṭabāʾī concedes impediments affect merit but rejects an analogy that empties angelic obedience of worth. Sāmarrāʾī specifies the righteous, faithful and God-fearing."}, {"id": "17:70/q10/p4", "position": "Humanity as a kind outranks even angels.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites the verse for this; Nasafī and Study Quran report a universal reading and Adam's prostration. Rāzī and Biqāʿī emphasize human potential. Zamakhsharī rejects this as forced."}, {"id": "17:70/q10/p5", "position": "Human messengers rank first, then angelic messengers, then ordinary angels above ordinary humans.", "reasons": "Hanafis, many Shāfiʿīs and Ashʿarīs are reported for this layered order; Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports a similar ranking."}, {"id": "17:70/q10/p6", "position": "Cherubic angels rank first, then human messengers, perfected humans, and ordinary angels above ordinary humans.", "reasons": "Ālūsī attributes this to Rāzī, with Ghazālī similar; Ṭabāṭabāʾī repeats it."}, {"id": "17:70/q10/p7", "position": "All perfected humans, including saints, outrank angels generally.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this third position. Kashifī refines it to human progeny over angelic messengers, human saints over angelic saints, good believers over common angels, and common angels over sinful believers. Bursevī invokes Adam's knowledge and the prostration command, 2:31 and 3:33, plus a report of an angel standing for Muhammad."}, {"id": "17:70/q10/p8", "position": "One should refrain from ranking angels against humans or prophets against one another.", "reasons": "A group cites reports against prophetic comparisons and preferring Muhammad to Jonah; Qurṭubī counters that the Qur'an itself ranks prophets."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q11", "question": "What does the report of angels requesting worldly or afterlife gifts say, and is it accepted?", "turns_on": "The report's chains and whether angels could meaningfully seek bodily pleasures.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q11/p1", "position": "Angels asked about human worldly pleasures; God distinguished righteous descendants of hand-created Adam from beings made by 'Be'.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Aslam's form is transmitted by ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī and Rāzī. Baghawī gives Jābir's prophetic version. Ibn Kathīr calls Zayd's form mursal and supplies connected versions through ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr and Anas; one adds human food, clothing, marriage, riding and sleep. Durr has a variant about riding horses omitting the breathed Spirit. Ṭabāṭabāʾī lists Ibn ʿUmar, Anas, Zayd and Jābir transmitters."

}, {"id": "17:70/q11/p2", "position": "The angels' request report is implausible or fabricated.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī calls it a manufactured prop for human superiority; Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues bodily needs are survival means for humans while angels already possess the perfection humans seek."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q12", "question": "How do honoring and favoring differ?", "turns_on": "Whether the two verbs separate innate from comparative gifts, worldly from afterlife gifts, means from outcomes, or simply clarify one another.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q12/p1", "position": "Honor is an innate unique dignity, while preference is comparative abundance in gifts shared with other creatures.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī makes intellect and its derivatives intrinsic honor, and more varied food, clothing, homes, family and society comparative preference; he rejects distinctions unsupported by ordinary language."}, {"id": "17:70/q12/p2", "position": "Honor is natural endowment; preference is the acquired true belief and virtue made possible by it.", "reasons": "Rāzī and Ālūsī say intellect, speech, writing, beauty and stature enable salvation through acquired beliefs and character. Ālūsī says simple identity of the two clauses would repeat the point; Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects restricting the Arabic terms so sharply."}, {"id": "17:70/q12/p3", "position": "Honor names worldly gifts, and preference names afterlife or spiritual gifts.", "reasons": "Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, al-Majmaʿ and Study Quran transmit this solution to apparent repetition; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says evidence for it is lacking."}, {"id": "17:70/q12/p4", "position": "Honor supplies the means for moral obligation; preference is the higher rank obligation enables.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ṭabrisī offer this; Ṭabāṭabāʾī quotes al-Majmaʿ and Ālūsī reports a similar account."}, {"id": "17:70/q12/p5", "position": "Honor is beneficence; preference is superior giving.", "reasons": "Al-Majmaʿ's formulation is quoted by Ṭabāṭabāʾī, who rejects making preference necessarily an undeserved gift."}, {"id": "17:70/q12/p6", "position": "Dignity is worth in itself, while superiority consists in reason, judgment, knowledge and sciences.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives this distinction between intrinsic worth and achieved or displayed distinction."}, {"id": "17:70/q12/p7", "position": "The clauses form an ascending sequence of honors, transport, provision and culminating preference.", "reasons": "Ṭībī says the angels' prostration explains Adam's honor, with intervening verses a digression. Rāzī insists the two expressions are not identical; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says carriage and provision are concrete instances of honor."}, {"id": "17:70/q12/p8", "position": "The second clause explains or repeats the first distinction.", "reasons": "Jishumī says karam alone signals blessing but not comparison, so faḍḍalnā makes the comparison explicit. Ālūsī reports identifying preference with the prior honor."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q13", "question": "What does the final tafḍīlan add grammatically and rhetorically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q13/p1", "position": "It is an emphatic verbal noun intensifying the preceding verb.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās identifies the cognate object; Ibn ʿĀshūr says its indefinite form conveys a great degree of preference."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q14", "question": "How does the verse connect with its surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the immediate link is rescue and warning, Adam's story, the afterlife, resurrection, or the later prophetic episode.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q14/p1", "position": "It follows danger at sea and warnings by recalling God's gifts and calling for gratitude.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān connects ships and rescue to honor and says the threat of drowning makes gratitude and obedience urgent. Qurṭubī says blessing follows warning. Ṭabāṭabāʾī sees a reproach for forgetting God after rescue; Kuranyolu and Study Quran stress natural power and punishment as sura themes."}, {"id": "17:70/q14/p2", "position": "It recalls Iblīs's complaint that Adam was honored and enumerates Adam's descendants' gifts.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī links the passage to the complaint and following honors; Asad sees continuity with 17:61 and Adam's knowledge at 2:31."}, {"id": "17:70/q14/p3", "position": "It leads from worldly honors to the following account of the afterlife.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān makes this transition; Burhān reports interpreting blindness in the next passage as inability to see afterlife bliss after denial of these worldly gifts."}, {"id": "17:70/q14/p4", "position": "Human distinction after the signs points to God's power to resurrect.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī argues that God differentiated creatures that began alike."}, {"id": "17:70/q14/p5", "position": "The later verses describe the Prophet's steadfastness when idolaters tried to divert him.", "reasons": "Study Quran summarizes 70–76 as nearly yielding to pressure before God made him firm."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q15", "question": "What practical response does the verse call for?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q15/p1", "position": "Gratitude, obedience, sound belief and rejection of idolatry.", "reasons": "Bursevī says discernment should lead to thanks and rejecting shirk; Ālūsī's al-Kashf says remembered care rebukes idolatry; Kuranyolu says familiar means of travel are divine favors. Islāḥī warns against Satan-like arrogance and assuming unlimited human superiority."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q16", "question": "Was the verse revealed after a journey involving roadside pools?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q16/p1", "position": "Some said it was revealed when the Prophet told companions to wash hands and drink from roadside pools rather than dip their heads.", "reasons": "Al-Furāt ibn Salmān relates the journey instruction; an unnamed group connects the verse's revelation to it."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q17", "question": "Does human honor affect the ritual status of a dead person?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q17/p1", "position": "A human corpse does not become ritually impure.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports al-Shāfiʿī using the verse as evidence."}]}
{"id": "17:70/q18", "question": "What other reports illustrate divine favor or human selection?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different events and degrees of favor.", "positions": [{"id": "17:70/q18/p1", "position": "Praise for being spared an affliction protects the observer from it.", "reasons": "Durr transmits ʿUmar's report: protection applies whatever the observed affliction."}, {"id": "17:70/q18/p2", "position": "God selected humanity within a sequence ending in Muhammad as the best of the best.", "reasons": "The reported prophetic selection runs highest heaven, humanity, Arabs, Muḍar, Quraysh, Banū Hāshim, then Muhammad."}, {"id": "17:70/q18/p3", "position": "An unusual report makes Adam's child dearest to God on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls the report very unusual; it says angels are compelled like sun and moon."}]}

{"id": "17:78/q03", "question": "What does the lām in li-dulūk mean?", "turns_on": "The cited sources differ over lexical scope, reports, grammatical construal or legal inference, as set out in the positions.", "positions": [{"id": "17:78/q03/p1", "position": "It marks the time, at the sun's decline.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn ʿAshur explain it as 'at'; Islahi also uses this temporal sense."}, {"id": "17:78/q03/p2", "position": "It means after the sun's decline.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi cite Mutammim ibn Nuwayra's elegy and the idiom for days elapsed; Burhan and Itqan give the same sense."}, {"id": "17:78/q03/p3", "position": "It marks the cause of the prayer's obligation.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi: the sun's decline causes prayer to become due; Ibn Aban calls this the apparent sense."}, {"id": "17:78/q03/p4", "position": "It is emphatic.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari compares 27:72."}]}

{"id": "17:78/q05", "question": "Which prayers does the sun-to-night span encompass?", "turns_on": "The starting sense of dulūk and whether a continuous span names every prayer time.", "positions": [{"id": "17:78/q05/p1", "position": "Decline to nightfall covers Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ; dawn adds Fajr.", "reasons": "Azhari, Baghawi, Tabarsi, Razi and others prefer noon because it encompasses all five; Gabriel's teaching supplies the individual times."}, {"id": "17:78/q05/p2", "position": "From sunset it covers Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, then separately Fajr.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud's sunset report grounds this reading; Ibn ʿAtiyya notes noon and afternoon then remain unmentioned. {"id": "17:78/q07", "question": "Which prayer is associated with ghasaq?", "turns_on": "Whether ghasaq points to sunset, the dark time of ʿIshāʾ, or the whole evening interval.", "positions": [{"id": "17:78/q07/p1", "position": "ʿIshāʾ, the final night prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud and several commentators associate darkness with ʿIshāʾ."}, {"id": "17:78/q07/p2", "position": "Maghrib, at the beginning of night.", "reasons": "Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Abbas associate the onset or sunset with Maghrib; Tabari prefers this over ʿAsr."}, {"id": "17:78/q07/p3", "position": "Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ.", "reasons": "Hasan and other commentators distribute both evening prayers within the interval."}, {"id": "17:78/q07/p4", "position": "ʿAṣr.", "reasons": "Tabari reports this minority view through Abu Jaʿfar and rejects it because ʿAṣr lies before nightfall."}]}
